turns.prompt_text: For making a beehive box they have this like puzzle piece interlocking pattern. I'm not sure what the best tool to do that would be. I also have chisels
turns.response_html:
That interlocking "puzzle piece" pattern is technically called a Box Joint (or Finger Joint). It’s the gold standard for beehives because it provides a massive amount of surface area for glue, making the corners incredibly strong against the weight of honey and the elements.

Since you are working with a circular saw, a handheld compact saw, a jigsaw, and chisels, here is the most effective approach:

1. The Best Tool: Handheld Circular Saw + Chisels

Using the smaller, more handheld circular saw is actually your best bet for precision here.

  • The Method: You’ll perform "kerfing" (making multiple thin passes).
  • The Setup: Clamp your boards together so you can cut the notches into multiple sides at once. Set the depth of your circular saw blade to exactly the thickness of your wood.
  • The Process: 1. Mark your "fingers" clearly on the wood. 2. Use the circular saw to make several parallel cuts within the area you want to remove. 3. The "Chisel Finish": Use your chisels to pop out the thin slices of wood left behind by the saw and pare the bottom of the notch until it's perfectly flat.

2. The Jigsaw Option

You can use the jigsaw, but it is often the most frustrating tool for this specific job.

  • The Risk: Jigsaw blades tend to "wander" or flex, especially in thicker wood. This leads to joints that are tight at the top but have gaps at the bottom, making the beehive box wonky or weak.
  • When to use it: Only if you have a very steady hand and a high-quality "clean cut" blade. Use it to cut the vertical lines, then use your chisel to chop out the waste.

3. Pro Tips for Beehive Boxes

  • The "Sacrificial" Board: When cutting with your circular saw, clamp a scrap piece of wood to the back of your project boards. This prevents the saw from "blowing out" the wood fibers as the blade exits, leaving you with clean, professional edges.
  • Tightness is Key: Aim for a fit that requires a light tap with a mallet (or a scrap block of wood). If it’s too loose, the hive might sag; if it's too tight, the wood might split when it swells with moisture.
  • Weatherproofing: Since this is for bees, ensure your glue is waterproof (Titebond III is the standard) and that any paint or finish you use on the outside is non-toxic.

Which wood are you planning to use for the hive? (Cedar and Pine are the most common, but they behave a bit differently under a chisel.)

turns.prompt_text: I'm planning to use pine. Although I'm not sure how to get that precision for the interlocking pattern or if it would be better to do more of a trapezoidal pattern rather than Square in your locks
turns.response_html:
For a beehive, pine is an excellent, lightweight choice, though it is prone to splintering if your tools aren't sharp.

What you are describing—the trapezoidal pattern—is known as a Dovetail Joint. While it looks beautiful and is incredibly strong, it is significantly more difficult to cut than the square Box Joint (also called a Finger Joint), especially with the tools you currently have.

Square (Box) vs. Trapezoidal (Dovetail)

FeatureBox Joint (Square)Dovetail (Trapezoidal)
StrengthVery High (due to glue surface).Highest (mechanical "lock" holds even without glue).
DifficultyModerate; requires consistent spacing.High; requires precise angles and "pins/tails" matching.
Best ToolCircular saw + Chisel.Hand saw + Very sharp chisels.

How to Get Precision with Your Tools

To get the precision needed for an interlocking pattern without a table saw, you should use a "Gang Cutting" technique and a Story Stick.

1. The Story Stick (Your Secret Weapon)

Instead of measuring every single cut with a ruler (where 1mm of error adds up quickly), take a scrap piece of wood and mark the exact width of your "fingers" on it. Use this "story stick" to mark every board. This ensures that even if your measurement is slightly off, it is consistently off on every piece, so they still fit together.

2. Gang Cutting

Clamp the two opposite sides of your beehive box together, face-to-face.

  • Use your handheld circular saw to cut through both boards at the same time.
  • This ensures the notches on the left side perfectly match the notches on the right side.

3. The "Kerf and Pare" Method

Precision with a circular saw comes from the "kerf" (the width of the blade).

  • Set your saw depth to the exact thickness of your pine boards.
  • Make your two outer "boundary" cuts for a notch.
  • Make several "waste" cuts in between those two boundaries.
  • Use your chisel to knock out the remaining thin "fins" of wood. Since it's pine, the wood will pop out easily.
  • The Secret: Use the chisel to "pare" (shave) the bottom of the notch flat.

Why the Square Joint is Better for You

The trapezoidal Dovetail requires you to cut at a very specific angle (usually a 1:6 or 1:8 ratio). A circular saw is not designed for those tiny, angled detail cuts. The square Box Joint allows you to keep your saw base flat and your cuts 90 degrees, which is much safer and more accurate for the equipment you have.

Do you have a speed square or a straight-edge guide to help keep those circular saw cuts perfectly vertical?

A speed square (also known as a rafter square or triangle square) is perhaps the most versatile tool in a carpenter's belt. It combines the functions of a square, a protractor, and a saw guide into one rigid piece of aluminum or plastic.

Since you are working with pine and need precision for those beehive joints, this tool is going to be your best friend.

Core Functions

  • The 90° and 45° Ruler: The most basic use is marking lines perfectly perpendicular or at 45-degree angles to the edge of your board.
  • The Fence: One edge of the square has a "lip" or fence. You can hook this against the edge of your pine board, allowing you to slide it up and down while maintaining a perfect 90° angle.
  • The Saw Guide: This is critical for your project. You can clamp the speed square to your board and use the flat edge as a fence for your circular saw. Instead of "free-handing" the cut, you press the base of your saw against the square as you push forward, ensuring a perfectly straight vertical line for your box joints.

Using it for your Beehive Joints

For your interlocking "puzzle piece" pattern, the speed square solves your precision problem in two ways:

  1. Scribing the "Fingers": You can use the markings on the square to ensure every "finger" is exactly the same width.
  2. The Pivot (Protractor): If you decide to try the trapezoidal pattern (dovetails) later, the speed square has a "Pivot" point at one corner. You can rotate the square to a specific degree mark (e.g., 10° or 15°) to mark those trapezoidal angles accurately across all boards.

Pro-Tip for Circular Saws

When using the square as a saw guide, remember to account for the offset of your saw. The distance from the edge of your circular saw's "shoe" (the metal base) to the actual blade is usually around $1\frac{1}{2}$ inches.

The Hack: Mark your cut line, then move the speed square back by that exact offset distance. Clamp it down, and your saw blade will track perfectly along your intended mark every single time.

Does your circular saw have a wide base plate on both sides of the blade, or is it offset more to one side?

    • The Caution: While a printed square is great for marking lines, be careful using it as a saw guide. If the spinning blade or the heat from the tool's motor touches the plastic (PLA/PETG), it will melt or nick the edge, ruining your straight line. If you print one, I’d recommend using it for layout and buying a cheap metal one for the actual cutting.

Using the Milwaukee Cut-Off Tool for Beehives

Because that tool uses a small 3-inch disc, it has a shallower depth of cut than a standard 7.25-inch saw.

A "No-Measure" Hack for Your Pattern

  2. Mark your first cut.
  3. Place the spacer block against your first mark to set the position for the next one.

Since you already have a speed square, you actually have everything you need to mark those trapezoidal Dovetail angles! You don't need to buy a different square; you just need to use the "Pivot" and "Degrees" features already built into yours.

How to use your Speed Square for Trapezoids

Standard dovetails for softwoods like pine usually use a 1:6 ratio, which is roughly 9.5°.

  1. Find the "Pivot" point: This is the small notch at the 90° corner of your square.
  2. Rotate to the Angle: Hold the pivot point against the edge of your board. Swing the square until the 9.5° (or 10° for simplicity) mark on the "Degrees" scale aligns with the same edge of the board.
  3. Mark the Slope: The long hypotenuse of the square now represents the trapezoid angle.

3D Printing a "Dovetail Marker"

If you want to try the trapezoidal pattern, I highly recommend printing a dedicated Dovetail Guide on your A1 instead of using the speed square for every line.

Since your Milwaukee cut-off tool is small, you can print a "saddle" style guide. These wrap around the corner of the wood, allowing you to draw the same angle on the face and the edge simultaneously.

  • Search for: "Dovetail Marker 1:6" on MakerWorld or Printables.
  • Why it helps: It ensures that your "pins" and "tails" match perfectly. If one angle is 9° and the other is 11°, the puzzle pieces won't fit.

A Warning on the Trapezoidal Cut

The reason beehive boxes usually stick to Square (Box) Joints is the assembly.

  • Square Joints: You can slide them together from the side.
  • Trapezoidal (Dovetail) Joints: They only slide in from one direction.

If you cut trapezoids on all four corners of a beehive box, you might find it impossible to actually "close" the box because the angles lock each other out. Usually, you'd do "tails" on two opposite boards and "pins" on the other two.

Precision Tip for your Milwaukee Tool

Because that 3-inch rotary tool has a very thin blade, it's actually great for the "Tail" portion of a dovetoid. However, it’s very easy to over-cut.

The "Stop Block" Trick: Clamp a scrap piece of wood across your pine board exactly where you want the cut to stop. When the base of your Milwaukee tool hits that scrap wood, it physically prevents you from cutting too deep into the box.

Since you are working with pine, a 1:6 ratio is the standard for dovetails because it provides a steeper angle that holds better in softer wood fibers.

Recommended 3D Models

You can find excellent versions of these on MakerWorld (which works natively with your A1) or Printables. Look for these specific designs:

  1. The "Saddle" Style Marker: This is a U-shaped bracket that slides over the edge of your board. It allows you to draw the angle on the front face and then immediately continue the line across the top edge.
  2. Magnetic Dovetail Guide: If you want to get really fancy, some designs include slots for small neodymium magnets. These actually hold your saw blade at the correct angle while you cut. However, these are usually designed for hand saws, and using them with a high-speed Milwaukee rotary tool might be risky for the magnets and the plastic.

Printing Strategy for your Bambu A1:

  • Material: Use PETG if you have it. It’s a bit more durable than PLA and can handle the friction of a pencil or the tool's base plate better.
  • Infill: Use a higher infill (around 40-50%) or more wall loops (4-5). You want this tool to be perfectly rigid; any flex will result in joints that don't line up.
  • Orientation: Print the marker on its side to ensure the "reference faces" (the parts that touch the wood) are as smooth as possible.

A Quick Trick for the "Puzzle Piece" Look

If you find that cutting the trapezoids is too frustrating with a rotary tool, you can achieve a very similar visual effect using "Box Joints" but making the fingers different sizes.

For example, instead of every finger being $3/4"$, you could make the middle one $1 \frac{1}{2}"$. This gives it a custom, "interlocking puzzle" aesthetic that is much easier to cut with your Milwaukee tool and a speed square, as you only have to worry about 90-degree vertical cuts.
